content: The capacity of institutions to produce new health workers can either be expanded or diminished, and new training programs for emerging cadres can be developed. This information is critical for identifying specific bottlenecks in institutional capacity, enabling targeted interventions to rapidly increase production when necessary. Monitoring the intake of students into health professional programs, as well as their pass and failure rates on licensing and certification exams, can reveal issues related to entry requirements, curriculum design, teaching methodologies, or other factors such as insufficient clinical placements. Each situation must be carefully evaluated to pinpoint the root causes of these challenges. Beyond the number of certified graduates, it is also essential to consider where these professionals choose to practice after graduation. High rates of attrition from the health sector or migration to other countries signal significant retention problems that demand immediate policy attention. Similarly, an overconcentration of new graduates in well-served areas and organizations highlights inequities in workforce distribution. In some cases, graduates may pass institutional proficiency tests but fail certification exams, indicating a misalignment between institutional training standards and certification expectations. In regions with severe shortages or uneven distribution of highly skilled health providers, mechanisms must be established to monitor the quality of large groups of lower-skilled workers who are trained to address the immediate needs of underserved and rural communities. These workers often serve as the first point of contact with the formal healthcare system and represent the system at the community level. Ensuring the quality of their training and practice through proper certification and supervision is therefore of paramount importance. Good governance and planning are essential for transforming health professionals' education. Governments must demonstrate political commitment at the highest levels and take leadership in implementing reforms. National plans for producing and retaining graduates should be developed in consultation with stakeholders, informed by labor market needs, and aligned with national health plans. Civil society organizations, particularly those in lowand middle-income countries, play a vital role in advancing transformative education initiatives. Research findings must be translated into actionable practices to gain the support of policymakers and advocates. Cost-effectiveness studies and capacity-building efforts for Southern civil society organizations are equally important. Standardized methods and metrics should be developed for transformational education research and practice. National agendas for civil society research and evaluation processes should be implemented to foster comprehensive policies that enhance the sustainability of the civil society workforce and leadership. Including perspectives from Southern civil society is critical for improving and scaling up health professionals' education. Tailored approaches to scaling up should consider contextual circumstances, with decentralized delivery and an integrated approach. Strong leadership and governance are required throughout the scaling-up process, and both state and non-state actors should be engaged as implementers. Underserved communities must be actively involved to ensure the success of scaling-up efforts. Knowledge gaps in the education and scaling-up of health professionals remain significant. Research must address these gaps with methodological rigor to produce evidence that is externally valid and actionable. Key questions include the impact of faculty development programs on teaching confidence, student learning, and clinical performance, as well as the effects of alternative pedagogical approaches like problem-based learning, simulation methods, and inter-professional education. The training needs of educators using innovative strategies and the impact of decentralized education on rural recruitment and retention also warrant investigation. Accreditation and regulation mechanisms must be evaluated for their effects on the quantity, quality, and relevance of health professionals. Factors influencing the success or failure of these mechanisms, as well as the feasibility and benefits of creating career ladders, should be explored. The costs and benefits of scaling up education and training institutions, as well as the financial incentives needed to maintain educator motivation, must also be assessed. Monitoring and evaluation of the scaling-up process require appropriate indicators to track progress and alert implementers to deviations from expected outcomes. Governance structures and mechanisms that sustain reform and maintain political and stakeholder commitment are critical. Research activities should focus on bridging knowledge gaps and supporting policy and decision-making processes. Examples include evaluating the impact of innovative continuing professional development methods, assessing the effects of decentralized education on rural recruitment, and studying the regulation of health professionals' education on practice quality and relevance.
